title: Wondering and looking closely: finding out what is inside a closed dabba

summary.text: You can find out what is inside a closed dabba without opening it. Shake it, lift it and tilt it, and the dabba gives you clues. Scientists begin the same way: they notice something, they wonder about it, and they observe closely with all their senses. Your child asks real questions, looks closely at one elaichi pod, and finds out what is hidden in three closed dabbas. They also hear how Inge Lehmann found a ball in the middle of the Earth that nobody has ever seen.
summary.art: A girl sitting cross-legged on a floor mat, holding a closed steel dabba to her ear and shaking it gently, with two more closed dabbas in front of her marked 1, 2 and 3.

intro.hook: A steel dabba is shut tight. You shake it, and it goes shhh, like rain. What do you think is inside? How could you know without opening it?
intro.text: You just found a clue with your ears. A clue is something you notice that helps you work out something hidden. Scientists are people who find out about the world. They start by noticing and wondering, just like you. Then they look, listen, smell and touch very carefully. In this unit you become a finder-out. You ask your own questions, and you work out what is inside closed dabbas.
intro.art: A child holding a closed steel dabba near one ear with eyes wide, while a grown-up in the kitchen doorway smiles and holds a finger to her lips.

outcomes: By the end I can ask a question about something I notice, starting with what, how or why.
By the end I can observe one thing closely with my eyes, ears, nose and hands, and say many things I notice about it.
By the end I can find clues about a hidden thing by shaking, lifting and tilting, and say what I think it is and why.
By the end I can check my guess, and say what I learned even when my guess was wrong.
By the end I can say how Inge Lehmann found out about the middle of the Earth without seeing it.

terms.meaning: A question is what you ask when you want to find out something. Many questions start with what, how or why.
terms.example: Why does the pressure cooker whistle?
terms.art: A small girl pointing at a whistling pressure cooker on a stove, with a big question mark floating above her head.

terms.meaning: To observe means to notice something very carefully, using your eyes, ears, nose and hands. A scientist observes before saying what something is.
terms.example: Rani, a girl in Class 1, watched an ant. The ant carried a crumb bigger than her own head.
terms.art: A girl lying on her tummy on a kitchen floor, watching one ant carry a sugar grain, her chin on her hands.

terms.meaning: A clue is something you notice that helps you work out something you cannot see. Scientists call clues evidence.
terms.example: Wet footprints on the floor are a clue that someone just had a bath.
terms.art: A trail of small wet footprints on a tiled floor, leading from a bathroom door to a towel on a chair.

terms.meaning: A scientist is a person who asks questions about the world, and finds out by observing and testing. Anyone who does this is doing science, children too.
terms.example: When you shake a dabba to find out what is inside, you are doing what a scientist does.
terms.art: A woman scientist in a lab coat and a girl in a frock, both shaking small closed boxes and listening, side by side.

explanations.definition: To wonder is to notice something and ask yourself a question about it: what is it, how does it work, or why does it happen?
explanations.description: You notice something and ask a question about it. Why is the sky dark at night? How does a spider make a web? Some answers are known, and some nobody knows yet.
examples: In 1921, C. V. Raman was on a ship and looked at the deep blue sea. He wondered why it was so blue. He found that the water itself sends blue light in all directions, not only the sky.
In the story, Kavya, a girl in Bengaluru, hears a tap-tap at her window every morning. She wonders who is tapping, and why.
A child sees the moon in the day sky and asks, 'Why is the moon out when the sun is out?'
explanations.context: This card is about how all science starts: with noticing and asking.
explanations.art: A man in a suit and turban leaning on the rail of a ship, looking down at deep blue water, with a thought bubble showing a question mark.

explanations.concept: Observing means using all your senses carefully
explanations.definition: To observe is to notice carefully with your eyes, ears, nose and hands, and to look again instead of only once.
explanations.description: A quick look tells you a little. A slow look with eyes, ears, nose and hands tells you much more. Never taste a mystery thing.
examples: One elaichi pod looks small and green. Look closer and you see lines on the skin. Shake it, and you hear the seeds inside. Crack it open, and a strong smell comes out.
A doctor listens to your chest, taps your back and looks in your throat. Each one gives her a different clue.
A cook in Kolkata listens to the oil crackle and smells the mustard to know when to add the fish.
explanations.context: This card is about how scientists look closely, using more than their eyes.
explanations.art: A girl holding one green elaichi pod very close to her eye, with a cracked-open pod and tiny black seeds on her other palm.

explanations.concept: Clues tell us about things we cannot see
explanations.definition: A clue is something we can sense that tells us about something we cannot sense directly. Scientists call clues evidence, and then they check them.
explanations.description: You cannot see inside a shut dabba. A shhh sound tells you there are many small things inside. Then you open it and check.
examples: A shut dabba that goes shhh when shaken probably holds rice, dal or salt.
Little holes in a guava are a clue that someone has been eating it, maybe a parrot or a squirrel.
Nobody has been to the middle of the Earth. Scientists found out what is there from the shaking of earthquakes.
explanations.context: This card is about finding out with clues, like in the Mystery Dabbas experiment.
explanations.art: Three closed steel dabbas in a row, each with a small drawing above: rain lines over the first, one round lemon over the second, and a soft cloud over the third.

explanations.concept: Other living beings find out about the world too
explanations.description: Every living being is aware of the world and finds out about it. A crow looks at a new thing with one eye, then the other. An ant taps a crumb with her feelers. A plant's roots sense water and grow towards water. Scientists still argue about whether they wonder the way we do.
examples: A crow on the balcony walks around a new shiny spoon, looks at it from every side, and pecks it once before picking it up.
Ants touch each other with their feelers when they meet, and find out who is from their nest.
A puppy sniffs every corner of a new room before settling down.

perspectives.who: Many scientists who study animal minds
perspectives.explanation: Crows, parrots, rats, octopuses and many other animals explore new things, even when there is no food. These scientists say this is curiosity, the wish to find out.
They say we can see that animals explore, but we cannot know if they wonder or ask questions inside, because they cannot tell us in words.

explanations.context: This card is about whether other animals and plants are curious too.
explanations.art: A crow on a balcony railing tilting their head to look at a steel spoon, while a line of ants below taps a biscuit crumb with their feelers.

agreed.text: Science starts with noticing something and asking a question about it.
agreed.evidence: Scientists' own stories of their discoveries almost always begin with something they noticed and could not explain, like Raman and the blue sea.

agreed.text: Clues can tell us true things about what we cannot see.
agreed.evidence: Doctors find out about your heart by listening. Scientists found out about the middle of the Earth from earthquake shaking. These findings were checked again and again by other people.

agreed.text: One quick look can fool us, so scientists look again and check.
agreed.evidence: Two dabbas can sound almost the same. Opening them, or testing again, shows which clue was right.

challenging.claim: You can only know about things you can see.
challenging.who: A common idea, and an old school of thought in India called Charvaka
challenging.for: Your eyes tell you a lot, and a guess from clues can be wrong.
challenging.against: Nobody has seen the middle of the Earth, or the air itself, but clues tell us a lot about both. Doctors find out about your heart by listening. When clues are checked by many people, we can trust them.
challenging.context: This card is about the idea that seeing is the only way to know.

challenging.claim: Insects are like tiny machines. They cannot see colours or learn.
challenging.who: Many scientists around 1900, including Carl von Hess, a German eye doctor, who said bees cannot see colour
challenging.for: Insects are small, and much of what they do looks the same every time.
challenging.against: Charles Henry Turner, an African American scientist who did his research while teaching school, showed around 1910 that honeybees learn colours and patterns. Karl von Frisch, an Austrian scientist, showed it again in 1914. Bees came back to the colour where they had found sugar water.
challenging.context: This card is about an old idea that insects cannot learn.

challenging.claim: A good scientist is right the first time.
challenging.for: Famous scientists are remembered for being right.
challenging.against: Scientists make many wrong guesses. A wrong guess that is checked still teaches something, because it shows which clue fooled you.
challenging.context: This card is about whether scientists are always right.

big_questions.q: You never saw inside the closed dabba, but you knew what was there. Did you really know, or did you only guess?
big_questions.hint: Think about your clues. How sure were you before you opened the lid? How sure were you after?

big_questions.q: When a dabba made no sound at all, was that a clue too?
big_questions.hint: What kind of thing makes no sound when you shake it? What does that tell you?

big_questions.q: Is there any question that nobody in the whole world can answer?
big_questions.hint: Think of questions about the stars, about the very start of everything, or about what an ant feels.

big_questions.q: Why do you think children ask so many questions?
big_questions.hint: Think about how much is new to you every day. Do grown-ups stop wondering, or do they wonder about different things?

story.title: The Tap-Tap at the Window
story.note: Bengaluru is a city in Karnataka. Paati means grandmother in Tamil. The magpie robin is a real black-and-white bird found in towns and cities all over India. Kavya, Arjun, Amma and Paati are made up.
text: Kavya was six. She lived on the fifth floor of a block of flats in Bengaluru, with Amma, Paati and her little brother Arjun, who was four.
One morning, Kavya woke up to a sound. Tap. Tap-tap. Tap. It came from the big window in the hall.
She ran to look. Nothing was there. There was only the glass, the curtain and the grey morning sky.
'Paati, someone is knocking on our window!' she said. 'But we live on the fifth floor.'
Paati was making filter coffee. She did not say what it was. Instead she asked, 'What do you notice? And what do you wonder?'
Kavya thought hard. 'I notice the sound comes from the hall window. I notice it stops when I come close.' Then she said, 'I wonder who is tapping. And I wonder why they stop.'
'Those are good questions,' said Paati. 'How could you find out?'
'I could watch,' said Kavya. 'But quietly, so I don't scare them away.'

The next morning, Kavya woke up early. She sat on the floor behind the sofa, very still. Arjun wanted to sit with her. 'Only if you are as quiet as a gecko on the wall,' she whispered. Arjun nodded hard.
They waited. Kavya could hear a pressure cooker next door, and a scooter starting far below. Then it came: tap, tap-tap.

A small bird was standing on the window ledge. He had a shiny black head and back, a white tummy, and a white stripe on each wing. He puffed up his chest. Then he flew at the glass and pecked it. Tap!
'He is fighting the window,' whispered Arjun.

Kavya looked closely. The morning sun was shining on the glass. In the glass she could see the sky and the trees outside, like in a mirror. And she could see a second bird in the glass. He was puffing up his chest too.
'He is not fighting the window,' Kavya whispered back. 'He sees a bird in the glass. He thinks another bird has come to his ledge.'

At breakfast, Kavya told Amma everything. Amma smiled. 'That is a magpie robin,' she said. 'At this time of year, the male birds chase other male birds away from the places where they make their nests.'
'Can you check if you are right?' Amma asked. 'What could you change?'
Kavya thought. 'If there is no glass, there is no bird in the glass. Can we open half the window?'

So the next morning, Amma slid one half of the window open. The magpie robin came. He hopped to the open half and looked in. He did not peck the air. Then he hopped to the closed half, saw the bird in the glass, and pecked the glass again. Tap!
Kavya grinned. Her idea had passed the test.
That afternoon, Kavya and Paati cut stars and moons from old paper and stuck them all over the glass. Now the window did not look so much like a mirror. The tapping became less and less.
Arjun pulled Kavya's sleeve. 'How did you know it was his own picture?'
Kavya counted on her fingers. 'First I noticed the sound. Then I wondered. Then I watched very quietly and looked closely. Then we tried something to check.'
'I want to find out something too,' said Arjun.
'Then start by noticing,' said Kavya. 'And ask lots of questions.'
story.epiphany: Kavya found the answer by noticing, wondering, watching quietly, and then trying something to check. Guessing alone would not have told her.
ask: What did Kavya notice first, before she knew it was a bird?
Why did Kavya and Arjun sit so still and quiet to watch?
How did opening half the window help Kavya check her idea?
art: A girl in pyjamas standing in a flat's hall, staring at a big glass window with a curtain, the morning sky grey outside.
A girl and her small brother hiding behind a sofa, peeping over the top, fingers on lips.
A black-and-white magpie robin on a window ledge, chest puffed, facing his own reflection in the glass.
A grandmother and a girl sticking paper stars and moons on a window, with the bird sitting calmly on a nearby railing.

games.title: Yes-or-No Detective: find the hidden thing with questions
games.players: 2 or more players. A grown-up reads the cards to anyone who cannot read yet.
games.context: This is a question game. One person thinks of a thing in the room. The others ask questions that can be answered only yes or no, until they find the thing.

printables.title: 12 question helper cards
items: Is it bigger than my hand?
Do we use it every day?

rules: The thinker looks round the room and secretly picks one thing. The thinker tells no one. If you like, the thinker draws or writes it on a slip, folds it, and keeps it to check at the end.
The detectives ask one question at a time. The thinker may only say yes or no.
Spread the question helper cards on the floor. Anyone may pick one up, and a grown-up reads it out. Put it back after asking. You can also ask your own question.
Each question gets one mark on the count sheet.
When a detective thinks they know, they point at the thing and say its name. If they are right, the round is over. If they are wrong, it still counts as a question.
If nobody has found the thing after 20 questions, the thinker says what it was. Then swap.
Everyone takes a turn as the thinker. The detective who found a thing in the fewest questions wins. With 2 players, compare your two counts, and try to beat them next time.

setup.art: Twelve small paper cards spread on a floor mat, each with a short question written on it, and a pencil and a sheet beside them.
setup.caption: 1. Spread the question cards on the floor.

setup.art: A boy holding up a card that says 'Is it soft?' while a girl sits with a folded slip of paper in her hand and smiles.
setup.caption: 2. The thinker keeps the thing secret. The detectives ask yes-or-no questions.

flow.do: 1. Spread the question cards. 2. Read three of them aloud. 3. Explain that the answer can only be yes or no.
flow.say: In this game, I think of something in this room. You find it by asking questions. I can only say yes or no.
flow.kid: Look at the cards. Each one is a question. The answer is yes or no.

flow.do: 1. You are the thinker first. Pick something easy, like a pillow. 2. Answer each question with yes or no. 3. Make a mark for each question.
flow.say: I have picked something. Ask me your first question.
flow.kid: Ask a question. Listen to the answer. Then ask the next one.

ask.q: Which question helped you most? Why?
good: 'Is it soft?', because then I knew it was a pillow or a cloth.
'Is it near the window?', because it took away half the room.

flow.parent: Children often start by naming things: 'Is it the fan?' Let them. After a few tries, show how 'Is it soft?' rules out many things at once.

flow.do: Swap. Your child is the thinker, and you ask the questions. Think aloud about why you pick each question.
flow.say: Now you pick a thing. I'll ask. Hmm, I'll ask if it's soft first, because that rules out lots of things.
flow.kid: Now you pick a secret thing. Say only yes or no.

check.q: Which question tells you the most at the start?
check.why: 'Is it soft?' splits the whole room into soft things and hard things. Naming one thing only checks one thing.

flow.think: What makes a question a good question?

games.title: Question Dice: roll a word, ask a question
games.players: 2 or more players. A grown-up reads the dice word and the card to anyone who cannot read yet.
games.context: This is a game for asking many kinds of questions. You roll a dice with question words on it, turn over a thing card, and ask a question about that thing that starts with the word you rolled.

printables.title: 6 question words for the dice faces

rules: Stick the six question words on the six sides of a dice, or write them on six slips of paper and pick one from a bowl.
Put the thing cards in a pile, face down.
A player rolls the dice and turns over the top thing card. If the word and the thing do not fit together at all, roll again.
The player asks a question about that thing, starting with the word on the dice. For example: WHY plus A crow makes 'Why do crows caw?'
Everyone claps for every real question. There are no wrong questions. Put the card aside.
If nobody at home knows the answer, put a star next to the question on the paper, to find out later.
The game is won together. You win when all 12 thing cards have a question. Then pick the 3 questions you most want to find out later, and write them down.

setup.art: A dice with small paper squares stuck on each side showing WHAT, WHY and HOW, next to a pile of face-down cards.
setup.caption: 1. Put question words on a dice, or on slips in a bowl.

setup.art: A boy holding a card that says 'The Moon' while his sister reads 'WHERE' on the dice and laughs, a grown-up writing on a paper.
setup.caption: 2. Roll a word, turn a card, and ask a question.

flow.do: 1. Make the dice or the bowl of slips. 2. Read the six question words with your child.
flow.say: These are question words. What, why, how, where, when and who. Every question needs one of them, or a yes-or-no start.
flow.kid: These are question words. Say them with me.

flow.do: 1. Take turns to roll and turn a card. 2. Help your child make a question with the two. 3. Write each question on the paper. Star any that nobody can answer.
flow.say: You rolled HOW, and the card says A seed. Can you make a question? How does a seed know which way is up?
flow.kid: Roll the dice. Turn a card. Make a question with both.

ask.q: Which question did you like most? Why?
good: 'Where does rain come from?', because I don't know.
'Who lives in a coconut?', because it is funny and maybe something does.

flow.parent: Clap for odd questions too. 'When does the Moon sleep?' is a real question: it leads to where the Moon goes in the day.

flow.do: Read back the starred questions. If none are starred, choose the 3 you most want to check. Pick one to find out about together later.
flow.say: These are the questions we want to find out about. Which one shall we try first?
flow.kid: Pick one question to find out about later.

check.q: You rolled WHY and turned over the card Ice in a glass. Which is a good question to ask?
options: Why does ice get smaller in a glass?
check.why: A good question starts with the rolled word and asks about the thing. Now you can watch the ice and find out.

experiments.title: Mystery Dabbas: what is inside, without looking?
experiments.context: In this experiment a grown-up hides one thing in each of three closed dabbas. You find out what is inside each one by shaking, lifting and tilting, without looking. Then you open them and check. Then you swap, and your child hides things for you.
experiments.question: Can you find out what is inside a closed dabba without looking? Which of your senses gives you the best clues?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Will you be able to tell what is inside without looking? Which sense will help most: your ears, your hands or your nose? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: All three dabbas are the same kind and size, so only what is inside is different. You shake each one the same way, three gentle shakes. You say your guess and your reason for every dabba before any lid comes off.

materials.item: 3 steel dabbas or tiffin boxes of the same size, with lids that shut well (or 3 empty plastic bottles with caps, wrapped in newspaper)
1 cotton ball, or a small ball of cotton from a pillow
3 small slips of paper marked 1, 2 and 3, and some tape
paper and a pencil for the results
a few small things from the kitchen for your child to hide, such as dal, salt, a steel spoon or a pinch of atta in a twist of paper

schedule.what: Guess, then shake, lift, tilt and sniff three closed dabbas. Say a guess and a reason for each, then open them and check. Then swap: your child hides things, and you find out.

experiments.record: Draw the three dabbas in a row. Under each, draw what you guessed and what was really inside. Put a tick when they match. Next to each, draw an ear, a hand or a nose for the clue that helped most.

setup.art: A woman in a kitchen, her back turned so a child cannot see, dropping a lemon into one steel dabba, with rice and a cotton ball beside two more dabbas.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up hides one thing in each dabba, out of sight.

setup.art: A girl holding a closed dabba marked 2 next to her ear and shaking it gently, with dabbas 1 and 3 on the floor in front of her.
setup.caption: 2. Shake each dabba three times and listen.

setup.art: The girl holding one dabba in each hand, arms out like a weighing scale, with a puzzled, thinking face.
setup.caption: 3. Lift two at once. Which is heavier?

setup.art: The three dabbas open on the floor, showing rice, a lemon and a cotton ball, with the girl pointing at her drawing of her guesses.
setup.caption: 4. Open the lids and check your guesses.

flow.do: 1. Go to the kitchen, out of your child's sight. 2. Put 2 big spoons of rice in one dabba. 3. Put a lemon in another, and a cotton ball in the third. 4. Shut the lids tight. 5. Stick on the slips marked 1, 2 and 3. 6. Remember which is which.
flow.say: I have hidden one thing in each of these three dabbas. You are not allowed to look inside until the end. Your job is to find out what is in each one.
flow.kid: Three dabbas. One secret thing in each. No peeping!
flow.parent: Use dabbas that look the same, so the outside gives no clue. Shut the lids firmly before your child shakes them.

flow.do: Ask for a guess and a reason. Write it down.
flow.say: Do you think you can find out what is inside without looking? Which part of your body will help most? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess. Can you find out without looking? What will help most?

good: My ears, because things make sounds when you shake them.
My hands, because I can feel if it is heavy.
Maybe not, because I can't see inside.

flow.parent: Any guess is fine. Do not say what is inside, and do not say which sense works best.

flow.do: 1. Your child shakes each dabba three times, gently, next to one ear. 2. Ask them to say a word for each sound. 3. Write the word down.
flow.say: Shake dabba 1 three times, gently. Listen. What does it sound like? Now dabba 2. Now dabba 3.
flow.kid: Shake each one three times. Listen. What does it sound like?

ask.q: What did each dabba sound like?
good: Number 1 went shhh, like rain on a roof.
Number 2 went bump, like a ball.
Number 3 made no sound at all.

flow.parent: Rice goes shhh, because many small grains hit the steel. The lemon gives one knock and a roll. The cotton ball is almost silent. Do not explain this yet.

flow.do: 1. Your child lifts two dabbas at once, one in each hand, and says which is heavier. 2. Then they tilt each dabba slowly from side to side and feel what moves.
flow.say: Hold two dabbas, one in each hand. Which one is heavier? Now tilt each one slowly. Can you feel something roll? Or slide? Or nothing?
flow.kid: Hold two at once. Which is heavier? Now tilt each one slowly. Does something roll?

ask.q: What did your hands tell you?
good: Number 3 is very light.
Something in number 2 rolled and bumped the end.
Number 1 slid like sand when I tilted it.

flow.parent: The rice and the lemon may feel almost the same weight. That is a real result. Tilting slowly helps more: one round thing rolls and knocks, many grains slide together.

flow.do: Your child sniffs at the edge of each lid, without opening it.
flow.say: Now try your nose. Sniff at the edge of each lid. Can you smell anything?
flow.kid: Sniff near each lid. Can you smell anything?

ask.q: Did your nose find a clue?
good: No, they all smell of steel.
Maybe a little lemon in number 2.

flow.parent: With the lids shut tight, most children smell nothing. That is a clue too: it tells us which sense did not help today.

flow.do: For each dabba, your child says a guess and the clue that led to it. Write both down.
flow.say: What do you think is in dabba 1? What clue told you that? And dabba 2? And dabba 3?
flow.kid: Say your guess for each dabba. Say which clue told you.

ask.q: Why do you think dabba 3 has that inside?
good: Because it made no sound and it was very light, so it is something soft.
Maybe it is empty, because I heard nothing.

flow.do: 1. Open dabba 1, then 2, then 3. 2. For each, compare the guess with what is really inside. 3. Ask the check question.
flow.say: Let's check. Open dabba 1. Were you right? Which clue helped? Now dabba 2 and dabba 3. If a guess was wrong, which clue fooled you?
flow.kid: Open the lids one by one. Was your guess right? What fooled you?

ask.q: You never looked inside. How did you know?
good: The sounds told me, and the rolling.
My ears and my hands gave me clues.

flow.parent: If your child guessed 'empty' for the cotton ball, praise the reasoning: no sound and very light is exactly what an empty dabba would do. Ask, 'How could we tell empty from cotton next time?'

check.q: A shut dabba goes shhh when you shake it. What is most likely inside?
options: Lots of small grains, like rice
check.why: Many small grains hit the steel at many tiny moments, so they make a shhh sound, like rain. One lemon makes one knock and a roll. A cotton ball makes almost no sound.

flow.think: What else could you find out about without looking at it?

flow.do: Swap. Your child hides one thing in each dabba, out of your sight, while you turn your back. Choose from dal, salt, a steel spoon or a twist of paper with atta. You shake, lift and tilt, say your guess and the clue, then open the lids.
flow.say: Now you hide something in each dabba, and I will find out without looking. I will think aloud about my clues.
flow.kid: Hide one thing in each dabba. Don't tell. Can the grown-up find out?
flow.parent: Think aloud as you shake: 'It goes shhh, so many small pieces.' A salt and a dal dabba may sound alike. That is a real result: say which clue could not tell them apart.

activities.title: One Elaichi, Four Senses: how many things can you notice?
activities.context: In this activity you observe one tiny elaichi pod as closely as you can. You use your eyes, hands, ears and nose, and count how many things you notice.

materials.item: 2 or 3 green elaichi (cardamom) pods from the kitchen
paper and a pencil to count what you notice

setup.art: One green elaichi pod on a steel plate, with a child's face bent very close to look at the pod.
setup.caption: 1. Look at one elaichi pod very closely.

setup.art: A woman's fingers pressing an elaichi pod open on a steel plate, showing small black seeds inside, and a child sniffing.
setup.caption: 2. A grown-up opens one pod. Look inside and smell.

flow.do: Put one elaichi pod on the plate. Ask your child to say one thing about it, after a quick look. Write it down.
flow.say: Take one quick look at this. Tell me one thing about it.
flow.kid: Look quickly. Say one thing about it.

flow.do: 1. Now your child picks up the pod and looks slowly, turning it round. 2. They feel it, shake it next to one ear, and smell it. 3. Make a mark for each new thing they notice.
flow.say: Now be a scientist. Look slowly. Turn it round. Feel it. Shake it next to your ear. Smell it. Tell me everything you notice.
flow.kid: Look slowly. Feel it. Shake it. Smell it. Say what you notice.

good: It is green with lines on it.
It has a pointy end.
It rattles a tiny bit, so something is inside.
It smells sweet, like payasam.

flow.parent: A pod can rattle faintly when shaken, because the seeds inside are loose. If your child does not hear it, let them shake it near the ear again.

flow.do: Press one pod with your thumb until it splits. Your child looks at the seeds and smells the open pod.
flow.say: I'll open this one. Look inside. What do you see? Now smell it. Is the smell stronger or weaker than before?
flow.kid: Look inside. What do you see? Smell it now.

ask.q: What changed when it was opened?
good: There are tiny black seeds inside.
The smell is much stronger now.

flow.do: Count the marks together. Ask what your child wonders about the elaichi.
flow.say: After one quick look, you noticed one thing. After a slow look, you noticed this many. What do you wonder about the elaichi now?
flow.kid: Count your marks. What do you wonder about it now?

good: Why are the seeds black when the outside is green?
Could I grow an elaichi plant from the seeds?
Why does it smell stronger when it is open?

check.q: When did you notice more about the elaichi?
options: After looking slowly and using more senses
check.why: Looking slowly, and using your hands, ears and nose too, gives you many more clues than one quick look.

activities.title: Sticky Questions: a wonder walk around the flat
activities.context: In this activity you walk round your home and find things you wonder about. A grown-up writes each question on a slip of paper, and you stick it on the thing.

setup.art: A girl pointing at a ceiling fan while a grown-up writes on a small slip of paper.
setup.caption: 1. Find something you wonder about.

setup.art: A small slip of paper with a question taped to a fridge door, and another taped to a potted plant on a windowsill.
setup.caption: 2. Stick the question on the thing.

flow.do: 1. Walk slowly through the home with your child. 2. Stop at anything they ask about, or ask 'What do you wonder about this?' 3. Write their question on a slip, word for word, and tape it on.
flow.say: Let's walk round slowly and find things you wonder about. Look at the fan. What do you wonder about it? I'll write it down.
flow.kid: Walk round slowly. Find things you wonder about. Say your question.

ask.q: What do you wonder about this?
good: Why does the fridge make a humming sound?
How does the water get up to our tap?
Why are the plant's leaves turning to the window?

flow.parent: Write the child's exact words. A question like 'Why is the fridge cold inside but warm at the back?' is a real science question, even if you don't know the answer.

flow.do: Read all the questions back. Sort them together into two piles: ones someone at home can answer, and ones nobody at home can answer.
flow.say: Here are all your questions. Which ones can someone at home answer? Which ones does nobody here know?
flow.kid: Listen to your questions. Which ones does nobody know?

ask.q: How could we find out the answer to one we don't know?
good: Look closely at it.
Ask a grandparent, an older relative or a teacher.
Try something and see what happens.
Look in a book.

flow.parent: Keep the 'nobody knows' slips for the Wonder Jar project.
flow.think: Is a question nobody can answer a bad question, or a good one?

activities.title: How Do You Know? Ask a grown-up
activities.context: In this activity you ask a grown-up a question about the world. Then you ask them a second question: 'How do you know?'

materials.item: a grown-up at home, or on the phone

setup.art: A boy sitting next to a grown-up on a sofa, asking a question, with the grown-up's hand raised as they explain.
setup.caption: 1. Ask a grown-up a question about the world.

setup.art: A drawing on paper split into three boxes: an eye, an ear listening to a person, and a hand trying something.
setup.caption: 2. Ask 'How do you know?' Draw how they found out.

flow.do: Help your child pick a question to ask a grown-up. It could be from the Sticky Questions walk.
flow.say: Pick a question about the world to ask a grown-up. For example, how do you know when rice is cooked?
flow.kid: Pick a question. Ask a grown-up.

flow.do: Your child asks the question, then asks, 'How do you know?' The grown-up answers honestly.
flow.say: Now ask the second question: How do you know?
flow.kid: Now ask: How do you know?

good: They saw it themselves.
Somebody told them.
They tried it lots of times.
They read it in a book.

flow.parent: Grown-ups often say 'Someone told me.' That is a good answer to talk about. Ask, 'How did that person find out?'

flow.do: Your child draws how the grown-up found out: by looking, by being told, or by trying it.
flow.say: Draw how the grown-up found out. Did they see it, hear it from someone, or try it?
flow.kid: Draw how they found out. Did they look, hear or try?

check.q: A grown-up knows rice is cooked when it is soft. How did they find out?
options: They pressed grains of rice, many times, and saw which were soft
check.why: They found out by observing and trying again and again. That is how a lot of kitchen knowledge was found.

projects.title: The Wonder Jar: one question a day
projects.context: In this project you keep a jar of your questions. Each day you take one out, and try to find the answer by looking, asking someone or trying something.

materials.item: an empty jar, tumbler or small box

schedule.what: Fill the jar with questions from the Sticky Questions walk and new ones. Take one out and find out together.
Add any new question. Take one out. Find out by looking closely.
Take one out. Find out by asking someone.
Take one out. Find out by trying something.
Take one out. Then draw your favourite answer from the week, and how you found it.

projects.record: A drawing for each question you found out about, with an eye, an ear or a hand to show how you found out.

setup.art: A glass jar with folded paper slips inside, standing on a shelf beside a pencil.
setup.caption: 1. Put your questions in the jar.

setup.art: A girl unfolding a slip of paper from the jar while a grown-up reads it out.
setup.caption: 2. Each day, take one out and find out.

flow.do: 1. Put the question slips in the jar. 2. Add new ones your child says today. 3. Take one out and read it aloud. 4. Decide together how to find out.
flow.say: This is your Wonder Jar. Every question you have goes in here. Let's take one out. How could we find out?
flow.kid: Put your questions in the jar. Take one out. How could you find out?

flow.do: Help your child find the answer by looking closely, if the question allows it.
flow.say: Today let's find out by looking. What could we watch, or look at very closely?
flow.kid: Today, find out by looking closely.

flow.do: Help your child find the answer by asking someone: a grandparent, a neighbour, or a teacher on the phone.
flow.say: Who might know the answer? Let's ask them.
flow.kid: Today, ask someone who might know.

flow.do: Help your child find the answer by trying something safe.
flow.say: Can we try something to find out? What will we do, and what do you think will happen?
flow.kid: Today, try something to find out.

flow.do: Your child draws the best answer of the week and how they found it.
flow.say: Which answer surprised you most? Draw it. Draw an eye, an ear or a hand to show how you found out.
flow.kid: Draw your favourite answer. Show how you found it.
flow.parent: Some questions will not be answered. Keep them in the jar. Say, 'Nobody here knows yet. That makes it a very good question.'

challenges.title: Count the Coins Without Looking
challenges.context: This is a puzzle challenge. A grown-up hides some coins in a closed dabba. You must find out how many there are, without opening it.
challenges.problem: A grown-up has put some one-rupee coins in a closed dabba. Is it 1 coin, 3 coins or 6 coins? How can you find out without opening the lid?
constraints: You may not open the dabba until the end.
You may use a second, empty dabba of the same kind, and some coins of your own.
You must say your answer and your reason before you open it.
materials: 2 steel dabbas of the same size, with lids
general: Shake it and listen. One coin clinks once. Many coins jingle.
Lift it and feel the weight. More coins are heavier.
creative: Fill the second dabba with 1 coin, then 3, then 6. Shake both, one in each hand, and find the one that sounds the same.
Hold both dabbas, one in each hand, and add coins to yours until they feel equally heavy.
challenges.your_turn: Now you hide some coins in a dabba for a grown-up. Can they find out how many, without looking?

setup.art: Two identical steel dabbas side by side, one closed with a question mark on it, and a small pile of coins beside the other.
setup.caption: 1. One dabba has secret coins. One is empty.

setup.art: A girl shaking one dabba in each hand next to her ears, eyes closed, listening.
setup.caption: 2. Put coins in your dabba until it sounds the same.

flow.do: 1. Out of sight, put 3 one-rupee coins in one dabba and shut it. (Next time, try 1 or 6.) 2. Read the problem to your child.
flow.say: There are some coins hidden in this dabba. It might be 1, or 3, or 6. Can you find out how many, without opening it?
flow.kid: Some coins are hidden. How many? Don't open it.

flow.do: Let your child try their own way first. If they get stuck, offer the empty dabba and some coins.
flow.say: What could you do? Here is an empty dabba and some coins. Could they help?
flow.kid: Try your own idea first. You can use the empty dabba.

ask.q: How will the empty dabba help?
good: I can put coins in it and see if it sounds the same.
I can make it feel the same weight.

flow.parent: Comparing a hidden thing with something you know is a real science method. Scientists compare unknown things with known ones all the time.

flow.do: Your child says the number and the reason. Then open the dabba and count.
flow.say: How many coins do you think? Why? Now open it and count.
flow.kid: Say how many. Say why. Then open it and count.

check.q: Your dabba with 3 coins sounds just like the secret dabba. What does that tell you?
options: The secret dabba probably has 3 coins too
check.why: When two dabbas of the same kind sound and feel the same, they probably hold the same things. Opening the lid checks it.

videos.title: Inge Lehmann, a journey to the centre of the Earth
videos.why: Shows how earthquake shaking travels through the Earth, and how Inge Lehmann found the inner core from it.
videos.check: Found by search: "Inge Lehmann, a journey to discover the center of the Earth" by Geopop, 4 minutes, 43 seconds. A parent may preview it.

videos.title: Why do birds attack windows and mirrors?
videos.why: Shows the real behaviour in the story: a bird mistaking their reflection for another bird, and why that happens.
videos.check: Found by search: "Wild Moments: Why are birds attacking windows and mirrors?" by wgaltv, 1 minute, 41 seconds. A parent may preview it.

videos.title: Are crows the ultimate problem solvers?
videos.why: Shows another animal observing closely and finding out about something new.
videos.check: Found by search: "Are crows the ultimate problem solvers? - Inside the Animal Mind: Episode 2 - BBC" by BBC, 3 minutes, 20 seconds. A parent may preview it.

quiz.p: Meera sees a snail on the balcony wall. Which one is a question?
opts: Why does the snail leave a shiny line?
quiz.why: A question asks something you want to find out. 'Why does the snail leave a shiny line?' asks. The other two only tell.

quiz.p: Farhan wants to find out why the ceiling fan makes a clicking sound. What should he do first?
opts: Watch and listen to the fan closely
quiz.why: Observing closely comes first. Farhan may see where the click comes from, and how often.

quiz.p: Which question can you answer by looking closely at one ant?
opts: How many legs does the ant have?
Who will win the cricket match?
quiz.why: You can find out by looking. The other questions have nothing to do with the ant.

quiz.p: To observe a flower closely, what should you do?
opts: Look at the flower from across the room, once
Look closely, smell the flower and gently touch the petals
quiz.why: Observing means using your senses carefully, and looking more than once. Each sense gives a different clue.

quiz.p: Which sense must you never use on a mystery thing?
quiz.why: A mystery thing might be unsafe to eat. Scientists taste only things they know are food.

quiz.p: A shut dabba makes almost no sound and feels very light. What could be inside?
quiz.why: A cotton ball is soft and light, so it makes almost no sound. A spoon would clink and a potato would thump.

quiz.p: You tilt a shut dabba slowly. One thing rolls and knocks the end. What is it most like?
opts: Lots of tiny grains, like salt
quiz.why: One round thing rolls and hits the end with one knock. Grains slide together, and cotton hardly moves.

quiz.p: Lakshmi guessed rice, but the dabba had dal in it. What is the best thing for her to do?
opts: Say which clue fooled her, and try again
quiz.why: Rice and dal sound alike. Knowing which clue fooled her helps her next time. That is how scientists learn from a wrong guess.

quiz.p: You guess what is in a shut dabba. Why do you open it at the end?
opts: To check if our clues led us to the right answer
quiz.why: Clues help us guess. Opening the lid checks the guess.

quiz.p: What did Inge Lehmann find in the middle of the Earth?
quiz.why: She found an inner core, a ball inside the liquid outer core. Later scientists showed this inner ball is solid metal.

items.p: Here is an elaichi pod, opened. Say a word for each part, and a grown-up writes it: the outside skin, the inside, and the seeds.
a: green, with lines, dry and papery
small, black and sticky, with a strong smell
items.why: A strong answer uses more than one sense for a part: what it looks like, what it feels like, or how it smells.
items.art: A drawing of an opened green elaichi pod with small black seeds inside, and three empty label lines pointing to the skin, the inside and the seeds.

items.p: Draw a line from each sound to what might be inside the shut dabba.
items.why: Many grains make a shhh. One round thing bumps and rolls. Soft things are almost silent. Metal on metal clinks.

items.p: In a story, Kavya, a girl in Class 1, hears a tap-tap at her window every morning. What is the best thing to do first?
opts: Watch quietly to see what makes the sound
Shut the curtain and forget it
items.why: Watching quietly is observing. It gives real clues. Kavya watched and saw a bird pecking at his own reflection.

items.p: Draw something at home that you wonder about. Then say your question out loud, and a grown-up writes it.
items.a: A drawing of one thing, and a question about it that starts with what, why or how.
items.why: A strong answer has a real question that the child wants to find out, such as 'Why does the fridge hum?'
items.art: A blank box with a small question mark in one corner.

items.p: You can find out about a thing without seeing it.
items.why: True. In the Mystery Dabbas experiment, sounds, weight and rolling told you what was inside before you looked.

items.p: Some sentences ask. Some sentences tell. Circle the asking ones in green and the telling ones in blue.
items.why: A question asks for something you want to find out. It often starts with what, how or why.

items.p: Three of these words can start a question. Which one cannot?
items.why: Why, how and what are question words. Mango is the name of a fruit.

items.p: Say out loud, and a grown-up writes it: in the Mystery Dabbas experiment, which clue helped you most, and why?
items.a: For example: the sound, because the rice went shhh and the lemon went bump.
items.why: A strong answer names one clue and says how it pointed to what was inside.

items.p: You smell something sweet from the kitchen. What is the best way to find out what it is?
opts: Go and look, and ask what is cooking
Say nothing and wonder all day
items.why: Looking and asking are safe ways to get clues. Tasting unknown things is not.

items.p: Ammu, a girl in Class 1, wants to know if her glass of milk is hot. What is the safest way to find out first?
opts: Look for steam and gently touch the outside of the glass
Put her finger in the milk
items.why: Steam and a warm glass are clues from the outside. They tell her the milk is hot without hurting her.

items.p: Nila and her friend Tara, two girls in Mysuru, shake a shut dabba. It goes shhh.

views.says: It is rice. I am sure. We don't need to open it.
It sounds like rice, but it could be dal or salt. Let's open it and check.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Why? Then say one thing the other girl has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks one side and gives a reason. For Tara: rice, dal and salt can all go shhh, so checking tells us which. For Nila: the shhh is a real clue, and rice is the most likely thing in a kitchen dabba.
items.why: Both girls use the clue well. Nila makes a good guess from it. Tara knows that some things sound alike, so a check makes sure.

items.p: Put Kavya's steps in order, from the story about the tapping bird.
items.why: Kavya noticed first, then wondered, then observed, then opened half the window to check her idea.

items.p: Nobody has ever been to the middle of the Earth. Say out loud how Inge Lehmann found out what is there, and a grown-up writes it.
items.a: She looked very closely at the shaking from earthquakes as it came through the Earth.
items.why: A strong answer says she used clues from earthquake shaking, the way we used the sounds from a shaken dabba.

items.p: A doctor wants to know if your heart is beating well. She cannot see inside you. What does she do?
items.why: The sound of your heart is a clue. A stethoscope helps her hear it clearly.

items.p: Draw an animal finding out about something new. Show the body part they use.
items.a: For example: an ant touching a crumb with her feelers, a dog sniffing, or a crow looking with one eye.
items.why: A strong drawing shows a real way an animal finds out, with the right body part.

items.p: A crow walks round a new shiny clip and looks at it from every side before touching it. What is the crow doing?
items.why: The crow gathers clues with her eyes before she touches it, as we gather clues before opening a dabba.

items.p: Draw a line from each animal to the body part they use most to find food.
items.why: Ants smell and touch with their feelers. Dogs follow smells. Crows spot food with their sharp eyes. A snake flicks the tongue to pick up smells.

items.p: You hear a drip, drip at night. Which question would help you find out most?
opts: Where is the sound coming from?
items.why: Knowing where the sound comes from tells you where to look next: the tap, the window or the roof.

items.p: Which of these can you NOT find out by shaking a shut dabba?
opts: If there is one thing or many
If the thing is hard or soft
items.why: Sound and movement tell you about number, hardness and shape. Colour can only be seen.

items.p: A friend says, 'If you cannot see a thing, you cannot know what it is.' Say out loud what you would tell your friend, and a grown-up writes it.
items.a: A strong answer uses the dabbas: we never saw inside, but sounds, weight and rolling told us. Opening the lid checked it.
items.why: A strong answer uses the child's own experiment as evidence against the idea.

applications: Doctors find out what is wrong by looking, listening to your chest and asking questions.
Earthquake scientists study shaking to find out what is deep inside the Earth.
Mechanics listen to a scooter's engine to find out which part needs fixing.
Cooks look, listen and smell to know when food is ready, like the sizzle of mustard seeds.
Security staff at airports use X-ray machines to find out what is inside closed bags.

spotted.text: A coconut seller in Kochi shaking a coconut and listening, to know if there is plenty of water inside.
spotted.art: A coconut seller at a roadside stall holding a green coconut to his ear and shaking it.

spotted.text: A fruit seller in Pune pressing a mango gently and smelling the stalk end to know if it is ripe.
spotted.art: A woman at a fruit cart pressing a yellow mango with her thumb and sniffing near the stalk.

spotted.text: A child in Guwahati watching rain drops race down a bus window, and asking which one will win.
spotted.art: A child's face close to a bus window with rain drops running down the glass.

spotted.text: A grandmother in Chennai tapping a steel vessel and listening, to know how much rice is left inside.
spotted.art: A grandmother tapping the side of a big steel rice tin with her knuckle and listening.

spotted.text: Crows on a balcony in Jaipur walking round a new thing on the railing, looking at the thing from every side before they touch it.
spotted.art: A crow on a balcony railing beside a bright plastic clip, head tilted, looking with one eye.

open_questions.q: What makes us curious, and why do some things make us wonder more than others?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists study curiosity in children and in other animals. They have found parts of the brain that are busy when we are curious. How curiosity really works is still not fully known.

open_questions.q: What exactly is in the very middle of the Earth?
open_questions.why_open: We know there is a solid inner core of metal. Some scientists think there may be another, different ball inside the inner core. They are still studying earthquake clues to find out.

open_questions.q: Do ants, crows and plants wonder about things?
open_questions.why_open: We can watch them explore and find out. But nobody can know from the inside what it is like to be them, so scientists still argue about what goes on inside.

ask_kids: What did you notice today that you had never noticed before?
What is one thing you wonder about right now?
If you shut your eyes now, what can you hear? What made each sound?
What is inside this? How could we find out without opening it?
How do you know that? Did you see it, hear it from someone, or try it?
What question would you ask a crow, if the crow could answer?

jokes.j: Why did the scientist bring a ladder to class?
jokes.a: She wanted to ask some high-level questions!

jokes.j: What did the dabba say when you shook it?
jokes.a: Stop it, you are rattling my rice!

jokes.j: Why are detectives good at science?
Knock knock. Who is there? Dabba. Dabba who?
jokes.a: Dabba-dabba-doo, please let me in, I can smell rice!

jokes.j: Why did the ant shake the dabba?
jokes.a: She wanted to know what was for lunch!

jokes.j: Why did the girl stare at the orange juice box?
What starts with 'why' and never stops?
Why did the magpie robin peck the window?
jokes.a: He wanted to win an argument with himself!

maths.problem: Divya, a girl in Class 1, looked at an elaichi pod. After a quick look she noticed 1 thing. After a slow look she noticed 5 things. How many more things did she notice with the slow look?
maths.explain: 5 take away 1 is 4. The slow look, with more senses, found 4 more clues.
maths.context: This is about the One Elaichi activity, where you looked at an elaichi pod quickly, and then slowly.
maths.why_maths: Counting what we notice shows how much more a slow, careful look finds.

maths.problem: In the Yes-or-No Detective game, Meenakshi found the pillow in 6 questions. Her brother Sai found the spoon in 9 questions. Who used fewer questions?
maths.explain: Count up from 6 to 9: 7, 8, 9. That is 3 more questions for Sai. So Meenakshi's questions found the answer faster.
maths.context: This is about the Yes-or-No Detective game, where you find a hidden thing by asking yes-or-no questions.
maths.why_maths: Comparing the numbers shows which questions were better at finding the answer.

maths.problem: Gauri, a girl in Class 1, guessed what was in 3 shut dabbas. 2 guesses were right. How many guesses were wrong? Which clue might have fooled her?
maths.answer: 1 guess was wrong. Maybe the cotton ball, because no sound made her think the dabba was empty.
maths.explain: 3 take away 2 leaves 1. A dabba with a cotton ball and an empty dabba both make almost no sound, so that clue could fool anyone.
maths.context: This is about the Mystery Dabbas experiment, where you found out what was in three shut dabbas without looking.
maths.why_maths: Counting right and wrong guesses tells us which clues worked, and which ones need a better test.

song.title: I Notice, I Wonder
song.note: Topic-level song for How we know L1

links.title: StoryWeaver, free picture books from Pratham Books
links.why: For the parent: free picture books in many Indian languages to read aloud. Search for books about curious children and asking questions.

links.title: Visvesvaraya Industrial and Technological Museum
links.why: A science museum with hands-on exhibits where children can try things and ask why.

links.title: Science City
links.why: A large science centre with hands-on exhibits, good for a family day of wondering and trying.

warmup.q: What do we call something that helps you work out what is hidden?
warmup.a: A clue. Scientists call clues evidence.
For example: what, why and how. Also where, when and who.

warmup.q: A shut dabba goes shhh. What might be inside?
warmup.a: Lots of small grains, like rice, dal or salt.

warmup.q: Who found a ball in the middle of the Earth, using earthquake shaking?
warmup.a: Inge Lehmann, a scientist from Denmark, in 1936.

warmup.q: What does it mean to observe?
warmup.a: To notice very carefully, with your eyes, ears, nose and hands.

founder: ideas/by_topic/how-we-know.md: the Grade 1 grid ('Curiosity needs courage and care'; 'New ideas must be tested, not just imagined'), used in checking every dabba guess by opening the lid, in the Wonder Jar, and in the story, where Kavya tests her idea by opening half the window. The founder's list of deepest discoveries starts with the idea that nature follows rules we can find out, which is the starting point of this unit.

This unit avoids what the other levels and nearby units use: the Level 3 unit uses the brown apple watch, window watches and Tycho Brahe; the Level 1 senses unit uses smell steps, a senses tray, a dark room, touch words and shaker pairs; other units use leaf twins, feely bags, ant sugar tests and fingerprints. So this unit uses mystery dabbas, one elaichi pod, question games and Inge Lehmann.
science: Inge Lehmann, 'P′', Publications du Bureau Central Séismologique International, Série A, Travaux Scientifiques 14 (1936): proposed the Earth's inner core from earthquake waves arriving where they were not expected.
Francis Birch (1940) and later Adam Dziewonski and Freeman Gilbert (1971): evidence that the inner core is solid.
C. V. Raman, 'On the molecular scattering of light in water and the colour of the sea', Proceedings of the Royal Society A 101 (1922), written after his voyage to Europe in 1921.

Charles Henry Turner, 'Experiments on color-vision of the honey bee', Biological Bulletin 19 (1910); Karl von Frisch's colour training experiments with honeybees (1914), against Carl von Hess's claim that bees are colour blind.
Birds, including the oriental magpie robin, often attack their own reflections in windows during the breeding season, treating the reflection as a rival.
The Charvaka (Lokayata) school accepted perception as the only valid source of knowledge and rejected inference.

roots.context: We have asked questions, looked closely at an elaichi pod, and found out what was inside closed dabbas. Now we ask what the Mystery Dabbas experiment tells us about knowing.

deep_truth.truth: You never saw inside the closed dabbas. Still, shaking, tilting and lifting told you what each one held. When you opened the lids, you could check your clues. People found out what is in the middle of the Earth the same way, without ever seeing it.
deep_truth.habit: We think we know a thing only when we see it. The test shows that sounds, weight and movement carry true clues about hidden things, and that we can check those clues afterwards.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Mystery Dabbas experiment, rice went shhh and slid, the lemon bumped and rolled, and the cotton ball was almost silent and very light. The child named what was inside from these clues, then opened the lids to check.

three.who_am_i: You are a finder-out. Your eyes, ears, nose and hands bring you clues all day long.
three.what_is_life: Every living being finds out about the world. An ant feels with her feelers, and a crow looks with one eye, then the other.
three.what_is_this_world: The world is full of hidden things, like the inside of a dabba or the middle of the Earth. Everything that happens leaves clues.

roots.thread: The lemon in the dabba was hidden, but you still found it. When you shook the dabba, the lemon knocked the steel, the air carried the sound, and your ear caught it. An earthquake works the same way: the Earth shakes, and machines far away feel it. A hidden thing that moves sends out clues that we can catch.

teachings.source: The blind men and the elephant, told in Jain teaching and in the Buddhist Udana 6.4
teachings.teaching: Some men who cannot see each touch one part of an elephant. One feels the trunk and says an elephant is like a snake. One feels a leg and says an elephant is like a pillar. Each one is partly right, and none has the whole elephant.
teachings.link: In the Mystery Dabbas experiment, your ears gave one clue, your hands another, and your nose maybe none. Putting the clues together came closest to the whole answer.

teachings.teaching: The Upanishad asks: what is it that is the ear of the ear and the eye of the eye? Something in you hears through your ears and sees through your eyes.
teachings.link: Your ears heard the shhh, but something in you put the clues together and said 'rice'. The Upanishad asks you to wonder about that knower too.

science.text: In 1936, Inge Lehmann used earthquake shaking to show that the Earth has an inner core, a ball inside a ball. Nobody has ever seen it.
Crows, parrots, octopuses and many other animals explore new things even when there is no food. Scientists still argue about whether this is the same curiosity we feel.

other_view.who: The Charvaka thinkers of old India
other_view.view: They said that only what we sense directly can be trusted. A guess from clues can be wrong, they said, so it is not real knowing. Many scientists answer that clues become knowing when they are checked again and again.

practice.title: Listening for clues
practice.say: Sit still and close your eyes. Breathe in slowly, and out slowly. Now just listen. Each time you hear a sound, hold up one finger. Don't open your eyes. After a minute, tell me each sound, and what you think made it. Now open your eyes. Can we check one of them?
practice.kid: Close your eyes. Breathe slowly. Listen. Hold up a finger for each sound. Then say what made each one.

ask: Can you know something is true without ever seeing it?
If your clues and your eyes told you different things, which would you believe? Why?
What is something nobody has ever seen that you would like to find out about?
roots.art: A girl sitting very still with her eyes closed and three fingers held up, while around her faint drawings show a pressure cooker, a crow and a scooter far away.

how_we_found_out.story: Nobody has ever dug to the middle of the Earth. The deepest hole people have ever made goes only a tiny way down. So how do we know what is in the middle? When there is a big earthquake, the shaking travels right through the Earth. Machines in many countries draw the shaking as wiggly lines. In the 1920s, scientists thought the middle of the Earth was one big ball of hot, liquid metal. Inge Lehmann, a scientist in Denmark, looked very closely at the wiggly lines from a big earthquake in New Zealand in 1929. She saw small wiggles in places where there should have been none. Something deep inside had bent the shaking and sent it there. In 1936 she wrote that the Earth must have an inner core: a ball inside the liquid ball. Other scientists checked her clues, and she was right. Later they found that this inner ball is solid metal. Inge Lehmann lived to be 104.
how_we_found_out.who: Inge Lehmann, a Danish earthquake scientist
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: The middle of the Earth is one big ball of liquid metal, with nothing different inside it.
